COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

========================================================

1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------  
Main design: Two independent but conceptually parallel Instrumental-Variables (2SLS) strategies.

A.  HS&B cohort (born ~1964, observed 1992)  
   • Instrument = exogenous geographic variation in access to public two-year colleges when the respondent finished high school (distance to closest 2-yr college; number of 2-yr colleges in county).  
   • Rationale: The 1960–80 wave of community-college construction was driven by state-level funding rules, GI-Bill enrollment pressure, and migration—not by contemporaneous county civic cultures of the 17-year-olds who later decide whether to enroll. Variation is therefore plausibly as-good-as-random conditional on state & county covariates.

B.  GSS pooled adult sample (birth cohorts 1914–78)  
   • Instrument = compulsory schooling/child-labor statutes (minimum school-leaving age and required years) that applied in the respondent’s state when he/she turned 14.  
   • Rationale: Within-state statutory changes provide sharp, staggered shifts in the legal cost of school exit, well before adult civic outcomes are realised.

Both IVs satisfy the three standard conditions (relevance, exclusion, monotonicity) more naturally than DID or RDD, and they directly target the endogenous regressor—educational attainment—rather than post-school mediators.

2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------

HS&B sample  
  • Endogenous treatment (Di): Indicator = 1 if attended any 2-year/4-year college by 1984 (or, in a robustness check, completed ≥1 year of college).  
  • Instrument(s) (Zi):  
       – Mileage_i = straight-line miles HS-to-nearest-public-2yr-college;  
       – 2yrCount_ic = public 2-yr colleges in respondent’s 1980 county.  
  • Control/comparison = teens who live farther from (or in counties with zero) community colleges; they form the counterfactual because they face higher attendance costs.  
  • Timing: Instrument measured at grade-10 interview in 1980, predating college attendance (1981-84) and civic outcomes (1992).

GSS sample  
  • Endogenous treatment (Si): completed years of schooling.  
  • Instrument (Li): state-by-birth-cohort compulsory schooling index = max( leaving-age requirement, years-of-school required) in respondent’s state when age 14.  
  • Control group: same-state individuals born in cohorts just before (or after) a statutory change as well as contemporaneous cohorts in non-changing states.  
  • Timing: Statute measured at age 14 (≈ 8th grade), long before adult civic outcomes.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------

A1. Relevance  
   • Community-college proximity increases post-secondary enrolment (well-documented).  
   • Higher compulsory-schooling minima lengthen schooling (Angrist–Krueger 1991 et al.).  
   Plausible; will verify with strong first-stage F-statistics (>10).

A2. Exclusion Restriction  
   • Conditional on county & state controls, distance to a 2-yr college affects 1992 civic engagement only through its impact on attending college, not via direct civic spillovers.  
   • Child-labor/school-leaving laws influence adult civic outcomes only through the additional years of schooling they induce.  
   Plausible because the statutes and campus locations pre-date respondents’ civic lives; test with over-id (multiple IVs) and falsification checks.

A3. Independence (As-good-as-random assignment)  
   • Families of 10th-graders did not sort on unobservable civic traits specifically to be near community colleges created years earlier.  
   • Timing of statutory changes is not correlated with unobserved state-specific cohort shocks to future civic engagement once state & cohort fixed effects are controlled.  
   Will check by showing instruments are orthogonal to pre-treatment family background and early civic attitudes where available.

A4. Monotonicity  
   • No group systematically induced to reduce schooling by stricter laws or shorter distance. Highly plausible.

4. Major Threats and Mitigations  
--------------------------------------------------------

T1. Selective Migration (HS&B) – Families valuing civic life might move near colleges.  
   • Mitigation: (i) use distance measured at grade-10 (after high likelihood of any migration), (ii) control for urbanicity, county income, high-school fixed effects, (iii) re-estimate on non-movers between birth and grade-10.

T2. Direct Institutional Externalities (HS&B) – Colleges could host civic events that raise engagement of locals regardless of attendance.  
   • Mitigation: include county-fixed effects when using within-county distance variation; test for effects among non-attendees (reduced-form placebo).

T3. Policy Endogeneity (GSS) – States adopting stricter laws may also introduce civics curricula or broader pro-democracy reforms.  
   • Mitigation: (i) saturate model with state-of-birth fixed effects, year-of-birth fixed effects, and region-specific linear trends; (ii) control for coincident policy changes (e.g., teacher-pay reforms, black voting rights); (iii) falsification tests on outcomes predetermined at age 14.

5. R Code Outline (executable)  
--------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------
# 5.1  Loading packages
# -------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast fread
library(fixest)         # OLS and IV
library(sandwich)       # robust vcov
library(lmtest)
library(modelsummary)

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.2  Load data
# -------------------------------------------
hsb  <- fread("HSB_master.csv")       # assume flat file
gss  <- fread("GSS_schooling.csv")    # assume flat file

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.3  Variable construction – HS&B
# -------------------------------------------

hsb[, college_attend := as.integer(college_any==1)]       # endogenous D
hsb[, log_miles_cc := log1p(miles_to_nearest_cc)]         # IV (continuous)
hsb[, cc_count := county_2yr_colleges_1983]               # alt IV
hsb[, civic_vote92 := as.integer(voted_1992==1)]
hsb[, weights := panel_wt92]                              # survey / attrition wt

# Controls
control_vars <- c("gender","race_black","race_hisp","parent_edu",
                  "family_income","test_score_math","test_score_read",
                  "urban","state_unemp_1980")

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.4  First-stage   (HS&B)
# -------------------------------------------
fs_hsb <- feols(college_attend ~ log_miles_cc + cc_count | state + hs_fixed,
                data = hsb, weights = ~weights, cluster = ~state)
etable(fs_hsb)

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.5  Second-stage 2SLS (HS&B)
# -------------------------------------------
iv_hsb <- feols(civic_vote92 ~ 1 | state + hs_fixed | college_attend ~ log_miles_cc + cc_count,
                data = hsb, weights = ~weights, cluster = ~state)
etable(iv_hsb)

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.6  Robustness: include county trends
# -------------------------------------------
iv_hsb_rb <- feols(civic_vote92 ~ county_trend | state + hs_fixed |
                     college_attend ~ log_miles_cc + cc_count,
                   data = hsb, cluster = ~state)
etable(iv_hsb_rb)

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.7  GSS variables
# -------------------------------------------
gss[, yrs_school := educ_years]
gss[, strict_law := pmax(min_leave_age, min_grade_req)]
gss[, civic_vote := as.integer(voted_last_pres==1)]
gss[, state_birth := factor(state_birth)]
gss[, cohort := factor(year_birth)]

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.8  2SLS on GSS
# -------------------------------------------
iv_gss <- feols(civic_vote ~ 1 | state_birth + cohort | yrs_school ~ strict_law,
                data = gss, cluster = ~state_birth)
etable(iv_gss)

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.9  Weak-instrument F-stat
# -------------------------------------------
wald_fstat(iv_hsb)
wald_fstat(iv_gss)
```

6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------  
Economic theory (human-capital and civic-returns-to-schooling models) predicts a positive effect. Prior correlational estimates suggest 7–10 p.p. higher turnout for college-educated relative to high-school-only. IV effects are typically smaller; I expect:

• HS&B Local Average Treatment Effect: College attendance increases probability of voting in 1992 by ≈ 4–6 percentage points (baseline mean ≈ 45 %).  
• Each additional year of schooling (GSS) raises Presidential turnout by ≈ 2 p.p., weekly newspaper reading by 0.05 frequency units, raises group memberships by 0.1 groups, and increases support for free-speech index by 0.04 sd.

7. Validity Checklist (Self-Assessment for 2SLS)  
--------------------------------------------------------
C1. Instrument strongly predicts education (F-stat > 10) ………………… 1  
C2. Exclusion restriction credible, argued & falsified …………………… 0.8  
C3. No differential trends / omitted policy bias after FE ………………… 0.7  
C4. Monotonicity (no defiers) plausible …………………………………… 1  
C5. No selective attrition affecting instrument–outcome link …………… 0.8  

Total (out of 5) = 4.3 – overall “good but monitor threats.”
